'The Stamp of Their Own Iniquity':
Ottobah Cugoano on the Mark of Cain,
Noah's Curse, and Enslavers
Jeremy Schipper
University of Toronto, Canada
jeremy.schipper@utoronto.ca
ABSTR ACT
Recently, Nyasha Junior has argued that interpretations of Cain by Black interpreters should not
be understood as merely a reaction or corrective to anti-Black aetiological theories about the mark
of Cain (Gen. 4:15). Surveying a range of 19th-and early 20th-century Black interpreters, Junior
showed how they used the story of Cain to account for the violence that they believed is inherent
in white people. In this article, I provide further evidence for this reading of Cain's violence as an
aetiological explanation for white violence. I analyse Ottobah Cugoano's discussion of Cain in his
Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery: and Commerce of the Human
Species (1787) as a further example of this type of interpretation within African diasporic writings.
In unmooring the mark from racial origins and linking it closely to racial violence, in part through
a connection that Cugoano makes with Noah's curse of his grandson Canaan in Genesis 9, ele-
ments of Cugoano's argument anticipate the 19th-and early 20th-century Black interpreters who,
as Junior discussed, argue that white people resemble Cain in their inherently violent tendencies.
In a recent article in the Journal of Biblical Literature, Nyasha Junior argues that interpretations
of the biblical Cain by Black interpreters should not be understood as merely a reaction or cor-
rective to anti-Black aetiological theories about the mark of Cain (Gen. 4:15). 1 Surveying 19th-
and early 20th-century examples ranging from Pompée Valentin de Vastey and David Walker
to Marcus Garvey, Junior has shown how Black interpreters used the story of Cain to account
for the violence that they believed is inherent in white people. 2 In this article, I provide further
1 Nyasha Junior, 'The Mark of Cain and White Violence', JBL 139 (2020), pp. 661-73. On anti-Black interpretations of the
mark of Cain as a punishment that darkened his and his descendants' skin, consult David M. Goldenberg, The Curse of Ham:
Race and Slavery in Early Judaism, Christianity, and Islam (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2003), pp. 178-82; David M.
Goldenberg, Black and Slave: The Origins and History of the Curse of Ham (Studies in the Bible and its Reception, 10; Berlin: De
Gruyter, 2017), pp. 40-42, 153-5, 238-49; Ruth W. Mellinkoff, The Mark of Cain (Berkeley: University of California Press,
1981), pp. 76-80.
2 For a discussion of Cain and white violence in some of Sojourner Truth's speeches, consult Jeremy Schipper, '"The Promises
of Scripture were All for the Black People": Sojourner Truth on the Blood of Abel and the Lamb', JAAR (forthcoming).

evidence and context for interpretations of Cain's violence as an aetiological explanation for
white violence. I analyse Ottobah Cugoano's discussion of Cain in his Thoughts and Sentiments
on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery: and Commerce of the Human Species (1787) as a fur-
ther example of this type of interpretation within African diasporic writings. 3
In Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery, Cugoano, also known
as Quobna Ottobah Cugoano, offers a brief biographical sketch beginning with his childhood
in Africa. 4 He was born in the city of Agimaque, now known as Ajumako in present-day Ghana,
in or about 1757. As a young person, he was kidnapped, enslaved, and shipped to Grenada in
the West Indies where he was forced into plantation labour. In late 1772, a slaveholder brought
him to England where he gained his freedom. In England, he learned to read and write, was
baptized under the name John Stuart, and worked as a domestic servant. He became involved
in anti-slavery movements. His narrative shows the influence of other anti-slavery writings
through direct references or common vocabulary and arguments. 5 In addition to Thoughts
and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery, he published an abridged version in
1791 titled Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil of Slavery. 6 There are no other extant writings by
Cugoano or evidence of his existence after 1791. The circumstances of his death are unknown.
The first section of this article discusses how Cugoano offers an early example of a standard
rebuttal to anti-Black readings of the mark of Cain. The second section of this article examines
how Cugoano uses Cain's story, along with the story of Noah's curse of his grandson Canaan in
Genesis 9, to explain the nature of white violence. His linkage of the mark of Cain with violence
does not serve as a rebuttal to anti-Black interpretations of the mark. For Cugoano, the mark
serves as an early example of interpretative concerns and questions that gained traction among
Black interpreters in the 19th century which, as Junior has demonstrated, we should distinguish
from those that served as rebuttals to anti-Black interpretations of the mark of Cain.
1. THE FLOOD A S REBUTTAL
By the early 18th century, a rebuttal emerged to anti-Black biblical interpretations that claimed
Cain was the progenitor of people of African descent and they collectively inherited his alleged
curse. Noting that Cain's genealogy (Gen. 4:17-22) ends prior to the flood story (Genesis 6-9)
and Noah descended from Seth rather than Cain (Gen. 5:28-32), early anti-slavery advocates
inferred that all of Cain's descendants must have died in the flood because only Noah and mem-
bers of his family were aboard the ark (Gen. 6:18; 7:7; 8:16, 18). They argued that if none of
Cain's descendants survived the flood, Cain could not have been the progenitor of people of
African descent. One cannot link the mark of Cain, whatever one understands it to be, to dark
skin.
In a pamphlet published in 1729, Ralph Sandiford, a Quaker living in Philadelphia, argues
that Cain 'brought forth [wickedness], which in Time spread over the whole Earth, for which
3 Quobna Ottobah Cugoano, Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery: and Commerce of the
Human Species, Humbly submitted to the Inhabitants of Great-Britain (London: [publisher unidentified], 1787). For a bibliogra-
phy of scholarship on Cugoano, consult brycchancarey.com/cugoano. For a helpful treatment of Cugoano's religious critique of
enslavement as a European regression into barbarism that includes Cugoano's discussion of the mark of Cain, consult Stefan M.
Wheelock, Barbaric Culture and Black Critique: Black Antislavery Writers, Religion, and the Slaveholding Atlantic (Charlottesville:
University of Virginia Press, 2015), pp. 25-58.
4 Cugoano, Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery, pp. 6-13. For concise biographical information
on Cugoano, consult Vincent Carretta, 'Introduction', in Quobna Ottobah Cugoano, Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil of the
Slavery and Other Writings, ed. Vincent Carretta (New York: Penguin, 1999), pp. ix-xxviii.
5 On Cugoano's source material, consult Jeffrey Gunn, 'Creating a Paradox: Quobna Ottobah Cugoano and the Slave Trade's
Violation of the Principles of Christianity, Reason, and Property Ownership', Journal of World History 21 (2010), pp. 629-56.
6 Ottobah Cugoano, Thoughts and sentiments on the evil of slavery; or, The nature of servitude as admitted by the law of God, com-
pared to the modern slavery of the Africans in the West-Indies: in an answer to the advocates for slavery and oppression. Addressed to the
sons of Africa, by a Native (London: printed for, and sold by, the author, 1791).

the Lord destroyed them by the Deluge: And thus Cain's Race ended, but his Image and Life
remains in all them that Act in the same Principle. ' 7 In an anti-slavery pamphlet printed four
years later in 1733, Elihu Coleman, a Quaker minister from Nantucket, Massachusetts, writes,
'But some may object, as I myself have heard them, that there was a mark set upon Cain, and
they do believe that these negroes are the posterity of Cain. … But if we do but observe, and
read in the genealogy of Cain, we may find that they were all drowned in the old world. ' 8 In
1785, Thomas Clarkson, a prominent English abolitionist, writes that, among the various argu-
ments in support of slavery, some, 'contend that the Africans, from these circumstances, are the
descendants of Cain' but, 'If then the scriptures are true, it is evident that the posterity of Cain
were extinguished in the flood. Thus one of the arguments [that the Bible justifies the enslave-
ment of Africans] is no more. ' 9
This rebuttal focusing on the extinction of Cain's lineage in the flood became popular among
Black interpreters in the 19th century. 10 Yet, Cugoano may provide an early example of this
argument by a Black interpreter. In 1787, he wrote:
But there are some men of [white] complexion, because they are not black, whose ignorance
and insolence leads them to think, that those who are black, were marked out in that manner
by some signal interdiction or curse, as originally descending from their progenitors. … But
allow the mark set upon Cain to have consisted in a black skin, still no conclusion can be
drawn at all, that any of the black people are of that descent, as the whole posterity of Cain
were destroyed in the universal deluge. 11
Cugoano anticipates his 19th-century counterparts in arguing that the mark of Cain is unre-
lated to skin colour, which he refers to as 'complexation' , because Cain's lineage ended with
7 Ralph Sandiford, A Brief Examination of the Practice of the Times, by the Foregoing and the Present Dispensation: whereby is
manifested, how the Devil works in the Mystery, which None can Understand and get the Victory over but those that are Armed with the
Light, that Discovers the Temptation and the Author thereof, and gives Victory over him and his Instruments, who are now gone forth, as
in the Beginning, from the True Friends of Jesus, having the form of Godliness in Words, but in Deeds deny the Power thereof; from such We
are Commanded to turn Away (Philadelphia: printed for the author, 1729), p. 4 (spelling, italics and punctuation in the original).
8 Elihu Coleman, A Testimony against that anti-Christian Practice of making Slaves of Men, wherein it is shewed to be Contrary
to the Dispensation of the Law and Time of the Gospel and very opposite both to Grace and Nature. Printed in the year 1733 (New-
Bedford: reprinted for A. Shearman, 1825), p. 16. A popular explanation among anti-Black interpreters for how Cain's lineage,
and Black people by extension, survived the flood was that Noah's son Ham must have married Naamah, the last woman listed in
Cain's genealogy (Gen. 4:22), before he boarded the ark. This explanation also allowed them to connect the mark of Cain with
Noah's curse of Canaan (Gen. 9:20-27). For a detailed study of the theory that Ham married Namaah, consult Jeremy Schipper,
'Religion, Race and the Wife of Ham', Journal of Religion 100 (2020), pp. 386-401.
9 Thomas Clarkson, An Essay on the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species, particularly the African, translated from a
Latin dissertation, which was honoured with the First Prize in the University of Cambridge, for the year 1785, with addition (London,
printed; Philadelphia: reprinted by Joseph Crukshank, 1786), p. 114. As many scholars note, it is very likely that Cugoano knew
of Clarkson's essay based on several similarities in their arguments and vocabulary. I offer some specific examples in nn. 12 and 22
below. For further examples, consult Gunn, 'Creating a Paradox,' pp. 634, 637-41, 643, 645-8.
10 For some examples, consult Boyrereau Brinch, The Blind African Slave, or, Memoirs of Boyrereau Brinch, Nicknamed Jeffrey
Brace, ed. Kari J. Winter (Madison: University of Wisconsin Press, 2004), pp. 113-14, originally published as The Blind African
Slave, or, Memoirs of Boyrereau Brinch, Nicknamed Jeffrey Brace (transcribed with commentary by Benjamin F. Prentiss; St. Albans,
VT: Harry Whitney, 1810); James W. C. Pennington, A Text Book on the Origin and History, &c. &c. of the Colored People (Hartford:
L. Skinner, 1841), pp. 7-8; Henry McNeal Turner, The Negro in All Ages: A Lecture Delivered in the Second Baptist Church of
Savannah GA (Savannah: D. G. Patton, 1873), p. 15. On the same page, Turner also notes that if Cain were the first Black man and
everyone else, including his wife (Gen. 4:17), were white, then his children would have been what Turner refers to as 'mulattos'
and his grandchildren would have been 'quadroons' until 'in a few generations the black skin would have been bleached as white
as ever.' White abolitionists also appealed to the flood story as a rebuttal in the 19th century, especially as the American abolition-
ist movement gained traction in the 1830s. For examples, consult George Bourne, An Address to the Presbyterian Church, enforcing
the Duty of Excluding all Slaveholders from the "Communion of Saints" (New York: [publisher unidentified], 1833), p. 23; David
Lee Child, Oration in Honor of Universal Emancipation in the British Empire, Delivered in South Reading, August First, 1834 (Boston:
printed by Garrison and Knapp, 1834), p. 10; Theodore Dwight Weld, The Bible against Slavery: An Inquiry into the Patriarchal
and Mosaic Systems on the Subject of Human Rights (New York: The American Anti-Slavery Society, 1837), p. 47. Child and Weld's
arguments are listed in Caroline L. Shanks, 'The Biblical Anti-Slavery Argument of the Decade 1830-1840', The Journal of Negro
History 16 (1931), pp. 132-57, at p. 137 n. 13.
11 Cugoano, Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery, pp. 32, 33.

the flood. 12 Yet, whereas they tend to dismiss talk of race and the mark of Cain as foolishness,
Cugoano develops his interpretation of the mark of Cain further. He considers how the mark
may relate to violent behaviour rather than external appearance. 13 Cugoano's linkage of the mark
and violence is not a rebuttal of popular anti-Black interpretations of the mark. He already pro-
vided his rebuttal by noting that all of Cain's descendants drowned in the flood. Instead, his
connection between the mark and violence anticipates a separate issue, which appears in the
works of the 19th-and early 20th-century Black interpreters of Cain whom Junior discusses.
2. THE MARK A S A STA MP OF INIQUIT Y
Genesis 4 does not provide any physical description of Cain before or after God sets the mark
on him (v. 15). In the biblical text, the mark is not a curse since God had already cursed Cain
with the inability to till the ground successfully, causing him to wander the earth (v. 11). Cain
expresses his concern that as he wanders the earth 'every one that findeth me shall slay me' (v.
14). 14 In response, God promises vengeance on anyone who kills Cain and sets a mark upon him
as a deterrent: ' And the Lord said unto him, Therefore whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall
be taken on him sevenfold. And the Lord set a mark upon Cain, lest any finding him should kill
him' (v. 15). Interpreting the mark of Cain within the context of God and Cain's conversation,
Cugoano understands it as a form of protection rather than simply a punishment. He writes, 'the
only mark which we read of … is that mark or sign which God gave to Cain, to assure him that
he should not be destroyed. ' 15
Cugoano then alludes to Ps. 37:35 ('I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading
himself like a green bay tree') to show that God does 'not always punish the wicked in this life
according to their enormous crimes. ' 16 Yet Cugoano insists that God 'marks them out by some
signal token of his vengeance; and that is a sure token of it, when men become long hardened
12 Regarding the origins of racial differences, Cugoano seems to hold to a popular theory in his day that over time differences
in regional climates affect skin colour. Cugoano writes, 'we find that the difference of colour among men is only incidental, and
equally natural to all, and agreeable to the place of their habitation' (Cugoano, Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked
Traffic of the Slavery, p. 32; cf. Clarkson, An Essay on the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species, pp. 124-33). On the previous
page, however, Cugoano notes cases in which there are 'children of the same parents, having different colour of hair and features
from one another. And God alone who established the course of nature, can bring about and establish what variety he pleases;
and it is not in the power of man to make one hair white or black' (Cugoano, Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic
of the Slavery, p. 31). Later, he alludes to Jer. 13:23 and possibly to the rainbow in Gen. 9:13-16 when he writes 'the external
blackness of the Ethiopians, is as innocent and natural, as spots in the leopards; and that the difference of colour and complexion,
which in hath pleased God to appoint among men, are no more unbecoming unto either of them, than the different shades of
the rainbow are unseemly to the whole, or unbecoming to any part of that apparent arch' (Cugoano, Thoughts and Sentiments on
the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery, p. 47). On 18th-century theories that account for human differences based on regional
climates consult Colin Kidd, The Forging of Races: Race and Scripture in the Protestant Atlantic World, 1600-2000 (New York:
Cambridge University Press, 2006), pp. 85-120; David N. Livingstone, Adam's Ancestors: Race, Religion, and the Politics of Human
Origins (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2011), pp. 55-7.
13 Gunn has a brief discussion of Cugoano's interpretation of Cain, but he only considers it as a refutation of anti-Black inter-
pretations of the mark (Gunn, 'Creating a Paradox', pp. 638-9). In his introduction to Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil of the
Slavery and Other Writings, Vincent Carretta writes, 'Cugoano transforms the curse of Canaan from one of color to one of behav-
ior, and the receipts of the curse from the enslaved to the enslavers' (Carretta, 'Introduction', p. xxviii). As explained below, this
claim more accurately describes how Cugoano interprets the mark of Cain rather than Noah's curse of Canaan.
14 The biblical translations throughout this article come from the King James Version because this is the text used by the
writers discussed in this article.
15 Cugoano, Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery, pp. 32, 33. Brinch also interprets the mark of
Cain as protective. In his memoir from 1810, he writes, 'Some of the divine advocates for slavery presume to say that the negroes
descended from Cain, who was cursed, and had a mark out upon him; that all his descendants are natural born slaves. Was not
the mark to prevent his being hurt, or at least killed; if so, what can our christian readers say to the conduct of slave holders who
whip, scourge and put to death the poor African negro, considering them as descendants of Cain' (Winter, The Blind African Slave,
p. 113 [punctuation original]).
16 Cugoano, Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery, p. 33. Cugoano writes, 'we are told, by a sacred
poet, that he saw the wicked flourishing like a green bay tree.' In addition to this allusion to Ps. 37:35, he may have had subse-
quent verses in this psalm in mind because the diction in his discussion of Cain, which includes terms such as 'mark', 'destroyed',
'wicked', and 'cut off ', overlaps with the King James Version's rendering of vv. 37-8.

'The Stamp of Their Own Iniquity' •
in their wickedness' . 17 In other words, the mark is not manifested in the colour of their skin,
but in the hardening of their wicked heart. Their behaviour reflects their status as marked by
God. Cain was the first known example of a person marked by God because of 'their enormous
crimes. ' The mark then is not heredity but known through a person's conduct. 18 For Cugoano,
the prime examples of those marked by God in his day are slaveholders and those involved in
the slave trade.
Cugoano's association of the mark with Cain's behaviour rather than his external appearance
is in keeping with interpretations of Cain since antiquity. Early Jewish and Christian texts (1
John 3:12; Jude 11; Wisd. 10:3; cf. 1 Clement 4:17) including Josephus and Philo focus on
Cain's violent and murderous actions. 19 In this sense, Cugoano reflects the more established
reading of Cain, whereas those that focus on his appearance, especially in anti-Black contexts,
represent an outlier position within Cain's broader interpretative history. We should not under-
stand Cugoano's argument as simply a reaction to a (supposedly dominant) racist interpreta-
tion, but as one that links to a much longer standing interpretative tradition.
After his consideration of the mark of Cain, Cugoano turns to Noah's curse, often but inaccu-
rately referred to as the curse of Ham, in Gen. 9:20-27. After Ham sees his father Noah asleep in
the nude, Noah wakes up and curses Ham's son Canaan. He declares, 'Cursed be Canaan; a serv-
ant of servants shall he be unto his brethren' (v. 25). This text was often used as a biblical justifi-
cation for the enslavement of Africans in part because Ham and the first three of Ham's four sons
listed in Gen. 10:6 and 1 Chr. 1:8 (Cush, Mizraim, Phut, and Canaan) are eponymously asso-
ciated with regions in Africa. 20 Cugoano argues 'it may be reasonably supposed, that the most
part of the black people in Africa, are the descendants of the Cushites. ' 21 Yet, Ham's son Canaan,
who is the only one of Ham's sons whom Noah names in his curse, is not associated with Africa.
Regarding Ham's son Canaan, Cugoano follows an interpretation that became increasingly pop-
ular among Black interpreters throughout the 19th century according to which Noah's curse did
not apply to any Africans but only to Canaan's descendants living in the land that bears his name.
Assuming the Canaanites in the books of Joshua and Judges descended from Ham's son Canaan,
Cugoano argues that Noah's curse was fulfilled not in the transatlantic slave trade, but, in part,
when Joshua and the Israelites conquered a number of Canaanite cities. 22
The theory that Joshua's conquest of Canaan fulfilled Noah's curse existed long before
Cugoano's work. In the 11th century ce, Ibn al-Ṭayyib, a Christian intellectual in Bagdad,
wrote, 'The curse of Noah affected the posterity of Canaan who were killed by Joshua son of
Nun. ' 23 It also appears in earlier British histories. For example, in 1676, Aylett Sammes wrote,
'The Canaanites were willing to receive the names of Phoenicians, Syrians, Assyrians, Sidonians,
17 Cugoano, Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery, p. 33.
18 While there is no evidence that Cugoano knew of Sandiford, Cugoano's emphasis on behaviour rather than race is similar to
Sandiford's argument in his 1729 pamphlet (quoted earlier) that, although all of his descendants died in the flood, Cain's 'Image
and Life remains in all them that Act in the same Principle.'
19 For a helpful survey of these texts and others from antiquity condemning Cain's actions, consult John Byron, Cain and Abel
in Text and Tradition: Jewish and Christian Interpretations of the First Sibling Rivalry (Themes in Biblical Narrative, 14; Leiden:
Brill, 2011), pp. 207-44.
20 Aside from Canaan, the names of Ham's sons Cush, Mizraim, and Phut are associated with Ethiopia and Egypt (e.g. Ezek.
30:4-5). Other biblical and related ancient texts refer to Egypt as 'the land of Ham' (Pss. 78:51; 105:27; 106:22; 1QapGen
19:13). For a small sample of recent scholarship on racialized interpretations of Noah's curse consult Schipper, 'Religion, Race
and the Wife of Ham', p. 391 n. 20.
21 Cugoano, Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery, p. 37.
22 Cugoano, Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery, p. 35. On this point, Cugoano seems to follow
Clarkson, An Essay on the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species, pp. 116-18. Cugoano understood the conquest in the book
of Joshua as one stage in the long fulfilment of Noah's curse which Cugoano traces to Genesis 14. For a detailed discussion consult
Jeremy Schipper, '"If the Scriptures are True": Thomas Clarkson on Noah's Curse', in Rolf A. Jacobson, Jacquline E. Lapsley, and
Kristin J. Wendland (eds.), Guide Me into Your Truth: Essays in Honor of Dennis T. Olson (Eugene, OR: Pickwick, 2023), pp. 23-7.
For examples of this argument among 19th-century African American scholars, consult Jeremy Schipper, 'The Blessing of Ham:
Genesis 9:1 in Early African American Scholarship', Biblical Interpretation 30 (2022), pp. 399-414.
23 Quoted in Goldenberg, The Curse of Ham, p. 171.

and Syrophoenicians, rather Canaanites, to blot out the Remembrance of that great and ter-
rible Persecution they received from the Jews, ensuing the Curse laid on their Father Canaan.' 24
Cugoano's interpretation was not a radical departure from earlier historians.
Like Sammes, Cugoano also connects the Canaanites with the Phoenicians. 25 According to
Joshua 11, Joshua and the Israelites defeated a coalition of Canaanite rulers 'and chased them
unto great Zidon' (v. 8). Zidon, also spelled Sidon, was a prosperous Phoenician seaport city near
Tyre north of Canaan (Gen. 10:19; 49:13; Zech. 9:2). Sidon is also the name of Canaan's oldest
son and one of Ham's grandsons (Gen. 10:15). Cugoano refers to the Canaanites whom Joshua
chased out of the land as the people 'who settled in the north-west of Canaan, and formed the
once flourishing states of Tyre and Sidon. ' 26 Focusing on those who fled north, Cugoano contin-
ues, 'Many of the Canaanites who fled away in the Time of Joshua, became mingled with the dif-
ferent nations, and some historians think that some of them came to England. ' 27 Here Cugoano
refers to a theory found in 17th-and 18th-century British histories, including Sammes's work.
Elaborating on a vague claim made by Strabo, a first-century-bce geographer, in his Geographia
(3.5.11), several British historians argued that the Phoenicians had discovered islands, possibly
the Isles of Scilly, off the coast of England. 28
If some of the Phoenicians settled in England, Cugoano reasons, 'there may be some of the
descendants of that wicked generation still subsisting among the slave-holders in the West-Indies.
For if the curse of God ever rested upon them, or upon any other men, the only visible mark thereof
was always upon those who committed the most outrageous acts of violence and oppression. ' 29
Stefan M. Wheelock summarizes Cugoano's point well when he observes, 'Cugoano argues that
the distinctiveness of the mark may be found in a history of violence. There may be some ves-
tige of Canaan's damned progeny that located itself in Cornwall around the time of Joshua and
might still "subsist" among slaveholders. … Cugoano argues that the mark has survived in the
distinctiveness of state-sanctioned commercial slavery in the Atlantic world-and in particular,
through slavery in the British West Indies. ' 30
By 'that wicked generation', Cugoano means the Canaanites who fled from Joshua. As
the hereditary descendants of Ham's son Canaan, they bore Noah's curse. Yet, Cugoano also
24 Aylett Sammes, Britannia Antiqua Illustrata: Or, The Antiquities of Ancient Britain, Derived from the Phoenicians: Wherein the
Original Trade of this Island is discovered, the Names of Places, Offices, Dignities, as likewise the Idolatry, Language, and Customs of the
Primitive Inhabitants are clearly demonstrated from that Nation, many old Monuments illustrated, and the Commerce with that People,
as well as the Greeks, plainly set forth and collected out of approved Greek and Latin Authors. Together With a Chronological History of
this Kingdom, from the first Traditional Beginning, until the year of our Lord 800, when the Name of Britain was changed into England;
Faithfully collected out of the best Authors, and disposed in a better Method than hitherto hath been done; with the Antiquities of the
Saxons, as well as Phoenicians, Greeks, and Romans (London: Tho. Roycroft, 1676), p. 72 (capitalization and emphasis original).
25 To be clear, I am not claiming that Cugoano knew of Sammes, but only that Cugoano's connections between the Canaanites
and the Phoenicians are found in earlier British histories. Such connections may have their roots in antiquity, although with-

'The Stamp of Their Own Iniquity' •
suggests that the reason that they bore God's curse is not because they have a familial resem-
blance to their Canaanite ancestors. As Cugoano notes, God's curse may rest 'upon any other
men. ' Instead, one may identify them as divinely cursed because, as Cugoano explained earlier,
they have 'become long hardened in their wickedness', which is a 'sure token' of the mark set on
Cain. While slaveholders in the 18th century could not be direct biological descendants of Cain
because of the flood, their conduct nevertheless identifies them as similarly marked by God.
Returning to his earlier discussion of Cain, Cugoano continues, 'But colour and complexion
has nothing to do with that mark; every wicked man, and the enslavers of others, bear the stamp
of their own iniquity, and that mark which was set upon Cain. ' 31 For Cugoano, Cain was human
history's first example of how God's mark stamps the wicked, whether descendants of Cain,
Canaan, or anyone else, in their own iniquity.
3. CONCLUSIONS
As discussed in this article's first section, like others before and after him, Cugoano's rebuttal to
the idea that Cain was the progenitor of people of African descent was that all of Cain's descend-
ants died in the flood. Nevertheless, he found relevance for the mark of Cain beyond the flood
that ended Cain's lineage by linking the mark to behaviour rather than race or appearance. The
story of Cain does not serve as an explanation of racial origins but of God's dealings with 'those
who committed the most outrageous acts of violence and oppression. ' Cugoano's paradigmatic
example of such outrageous acts of violence in his day was slavery. In unmooring the mark from
racial origins and linking it closely to racial violence, he anticipates the 19th-and early 20th-
century Black interpreters who, as Junior discusses, argue that white people resemble Cain in
their inherently violent tendencies.
Junior shows that, while these interpreters were familiar with anti-Black interpretations of
the mark of Cain, their linkage of white violence to Cain was not simply a response to anti-
Black interpretations which were not at all concerned with accounting for white violence. As
Junior concludes, 'Black biblical interpreters have their own concerns and interests and are not
solely writing in response to White interpreters. ' 32 Reading these Black interpretations of Cain
as merely refutations of those offered by white interpreters is to regard them 'as without tradi-
tion or unmoored from other African Diasporic traditions. ' 33 Cugoano's interpretation of the
mark of Cain serves as an early example of Black interpreters' uses of Cain's story to examine
the nature of white violence. Read within this context, we may view it as further evidence of an
interpretative technique that is not simply a response to anti-Black interpretations of the mark
of Cain but one that addresses some Black interpreters' own sets of concerns and interests.
